title: The asymptotic Gotsman–Linial conjecture
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
formal: Is there a universal constant C>0 such that, for every n≥1, every integer 1≤d≤n and every Boolean polynomial threshold function f=sign(p):{−1,1}^n→{−1,1} of degree at most d, its total influence satisfies I(f)≤C d√n?
definitions: A realizing polynomial p is a real polynomial in n variables of total degree at most d, with p(x)≠0 at every Boolean input. The sign is +1 for positive values and −1 for negative values. Coefficients are unrestricted real numbers; no bound on coefficient magnitude, description length, margin or number of monomials is assumed. One may take p multilinear by reducing x_i² to 1 on the cube. The nonzero convention loses no threshold functions under a fixed sign-at-zero convention, since a sufficiently small constant perturbation preserves all assigned signs. If x is uniform on {−1,1}^n, let x^(i) denote x with coordinate i flipped. Define Inf_i(f)=Pr[f(x)≠f(x^(i))], pointwise sensitivity s_f(x)=|{i:f(x)≠f(x^(i))}|, and I(f)=Σ_i Inf_i(f)=E[s_f(x)]. The constant C is independent of n,d,f and the realizing polynomial. Constant functions have zero influence; allowing d=0 adds only these trivial cases. This is the asymptotic influence conjecture, not the disproved claim specifying an exact extremizing function.
answer_criterion: Prove one universal C works for all n,d and all such functions, or show that the ratios I(f)/(d√n) are unbounded over this class. A counterexample to a particular proposed numerical C, or to the original exact symmetric extremizer, does not by itself refute this existential-constant statement. A bound C_d√n with unrestricted dependence on d, or √n times a growing polylogarithmic factor, is partial progress rather than the claimed uniform bound.
context:
A polynomial threshold function first evaluates a low-degree real polynomial and then keeps only its sign. Linear threshold functions include majority votes and weighted voting rules. Quadratic threshold functions can also include pairwise interactions between inputs. The conjecture asks whether this algebraic simplicity forces the function to change its output relatively rarely along the edges of the Boolean cube.

Total influence counts those changes in an averaged way. If D is the number of undirected cube edges joining opposite outputs, then I(f)=2D/2^n. The maximum possible influence of an arbitrary Boolean function is n, achieved by parity. A degree-d bound of C d√n would sharply restrict the boundary when d is small compared with √n; once d≥√n, the elementary bound I(f)≤n already suffices with C=1.

Majority shows why a square root is unavoidable. For odd n, flipping a coordinate changes majority exactly when the other n−1 coordinates split evenly, giving I(MAJ_n)=n·binom(n−1,(n−1)/2)/2^(n−1), asymptotic to √(2n/π). Thus even degree one permits influence growing with dimension. The target is not a constant influence bound for every fixed-degree function.

There is a natural higher-degree candidate: place d parallel threshold hyperplanes between consecutive central Hamming layers, then take the sign of the product of their linear equations. The sign alternates at those layers. When the layers lie near the center, their boundaries together have order d√n. Gotsman and Linial proposed the much stronger assertion that this symmetric construction maximizes influence exactly.

Chapman disproved that exact assertion for most parameter pairs, including quadratic examples in every odd dimension at least five. The paper carefully separates its exact conjecture from Conjecture 1.2, the asymptotic statement used here, and leaves the latter open. Its SODA publication was in 2018; the arXiv copy was uploaded in 2021. Neither date turns the disproved exact formulation into a refutation of the remaining asymptotic question.

Products of d linear threshold signs satisfy the desired order by a simple union bound: if the product changes across an edge, at least one factor changes. Summing the factors’ influence bounds gives O(d√n). But a general degree-d polynomial need not factor into d linear forms, and its sign need not admit such a representation. This identifies one tempting argument and the missing structural fact it would need.

Kane proved the near-optimal dimensional estimate I(f)≤√n·(log n)^{O(d log d)}·2^{O(d² log d)} for d≥2. For each fixed d, this is √n times a polylogarithmic factor, establishing the correct exponent of n. The extra logarithms can still grow without bound, while the dependence on d is much larger than linear. Removing these losses is exactly what the displayed conjecture demands.

The proof program uses random restrictions and comparisons between Boolean and Gaussian polynomial behavior. Anti-concentration helps ensure that a small perturbation rarely carries the polynomial through zero. Such transfers must deal with coordinates of high influence and with the discrete cube’s concentrated mass. The continuous analogue is informative, but it is not a direct proof for arbitrary Boolean threshold polynomials.

For quadratic functions there are useful structural subcases. Kim, Maldonado and Wellens analyze the graph whose edges indicate nonzero quadratic coefficients and establish asymptotic estimates under restrictions such as low fractional chromatic number or few edges. This connects the influence question to the interaction graph, while leaving general dense quadratic interactions outside those special guarantees.

A 2026 paper by Chang, Slote, Volberg and Zhang proves a polylogarithmic bound, for fixed degree, on Boolean surface area BSA(f)=E[√s_f(x)]. The April 27 revision strengthens its original subpolynomial estimate. This is significant new control of boundary geometry, but BSA is a different moment from I(f)=E[s_f(x)]. A bound on the expectation of the square root does not directly bound the expectation by its square.

Indeed, pointwise s_f(x)≤√n·√s_f(x) yields only I(f)≤√n·BSA(f). Substituting the new polylogarithmic surface-area bound still leaves a factor depending on log n, with degree-dependent constants. This calculation explains why that recent theorem is compatible with the influence conjecture remaining open, without diminishing its improvement for the different boundary measure.

Kothari, Kovacs-Deak, Wang and Yang’s April 2026 revision on rational degree also restates the influence conjecture and proposes a weaker version using nondeterministic degree. Their theorem resolves a separate polynomial relation between rational and ordinary degree, rather than this threshold-degree inequality. These connections help explain the conjecture’s importance for the relationships among Boolean complexity measures, in addition to its learning and circuit applications.
why: A basic unresolved relation between algebraic threshold complexity and the edge boundary of a Boolean function, central to noise sensitivity, learning and threshold-circuit analysis.

importance.reason: A foundational and quantitatively sharp Boolean-function conjecture whose surviving asymptotic form matters even though the original exact extremizer was disproved.

progress.text: Kane establishes the correct √n exponent up to degree-dependent polylogarithmic factors.
Kim–Maldonado–Wellens establish influence estimates for structured quadratic coefficient graphs.
Chapman disproves the original exact extremizer conjecture while preserving the asymptotic open question.
Chapman’s MIT thesis again distinguishes the exact, asymptotic and weaker polylogarithmic formulations.
Kothari and coauthors’ revised rational-degree paper restates the conjecture and proposes a weaker nondeterministic-degree analogue in §5.2.
Chang and coauthors’ second revision proves polylogarithmic Boolean surface area for fixed-degree PTFs, a different moment from total influence.

status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The exact symmetric-maximizer conjecture is false, but the universal O(d√n) influence bound remains open in the checked primary literature, including the April 2026 revisions on rational degree and Boolean surface area.
